title: Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment
intro: This guide explains what Ontario's Construction Act says about who can claim a construction lien, holdbacks, the time limits for preserving and perfecting a lien, where lien actions are heard, prompt payment and adjudication. Numbers are given exactly as the Act states them.

sections.heading: Who can claim a lien
paragraphs: “A person who supplies services or materials to an improvement for an owner, contractor or subcontractor, has a lien upon the interest of the owner in the premises improved for the price of those services or materials.” (Construction Act, s. 14 (1))

An “improvement” means, in respect of any land, “any alteration, addition or capital repair to the land”, “any construction, erection or installation on the land” (including some equipment the Act describes), or “the complete or partial demolition or removal of any building, structure or works on the land”. (Construction Act, s. 1 (1), “improvement”)

“A person's lien arises and takes effect when the person first supplies services or materials to the improvement.” No person is entitled to a lien “for any interest on the amount owed to the person”, but this does not affect any right the person may otherwise have to recover that interest. (Construction Act, ss. 15, 14 (2))

A lien “does not attach to the interest in a premises of”, “the Crown” or “a municipality”. Where either has an interest in a premises but is not an owner, “the lien may attach to the interest of any other person in the premises.” Where the owner is the Crown or a municipality, or the premises is a railway right-of-way, the lien does not attach to the premises but “constitutes a charge under section 21”. (Construction Act, s. 16)

These rules do not apply to every project. The Act and regulations “as they read on June 29, 2018, continue to apply” to an improvement if, for example, “a contract for the improvement was entered into before July 1, 2018” or the owner commenced a procurement process for it before that date. The prompt payment and adjudication Parts (I.1 and II.1) also do not apply to certain older contracts and their subcontracts, as the Act lists. (Construction Act, s. 87.3 (1), (4))

sections.heading: Holdbacks
paragraphs: “Each payer upon a contract or subcontract under which a lien may arise shall retain a holdback equal to 10 per cent of the price of the services or materials as they are actually supplied under the contract or subcontract until all liens that may be claimed against the holdback in respect of the supplied services or materials have expired or been satisfied, discharged or otherwise provided for under this Act.” (Construction Act, s. 22 (1))

Where a contract has been certified or declared substantially performed but work remains, the payer keeps “a separate holdback equal to 10 per cent of the price of the remaining services or materials”. The duty to keep holdbacks applies “irrespective of whether the contract or subcontract provides for partial payments or payment on completion.” (Construction Act, s. 22 (2), (3))

Subject to limits, an owner “is personally liable for holdbacks that the owner is required to retain under this Part to those lien claimants who have valid liens against the owner's interest in the premises.” Where the defaulting payer is the contractor, that liability “does not exceed the holdbacks the owner is required to retain”. Where it is a subcontractor, a lower cap can apply. This liability “may only be determined by an action under this Act.” (Construction Act, s. 23)

sections.heading: Preserving a lien and the time limits
paragraphs: “Unless preserved under section 34, the liens arising from the supply of services or materials to an improvement expire as provided in this section.” (Construction Act, s. 31 (1))

A contractor's lien for work up to substantial performance “expires at the conclusion of the 60-day period next following the occurrence of the earlier of” the date a copy of the certificate or declaration of substantial performance “is published as provided in section 32”, and “the date the contract is completed, abandoned or terminated”. (Construction Act, s. 31 (2) (a))

For other lien claimants, such as subcontractors and suppliers, the lien for work up to substantial performance expires at the end of a 60-day period following “the earliest of” publication of the certificate or declaration, “the date on which the person last supplies services or materials to the improvement”, the date the contract is completed, abandoned or terminated, and the date a subcontract is certified complete under section 33, where the services or materials were supplied under that subcontract. (Construction Act, s. 31 (3) (a))

Where there is no certificate or declaration, or for work after substantial performance, a contractor's lien expires “at the conclusion of the 60-day period next following the occurrence of the earlier of” the date the contract is completed and the date it is abandoned or terminated. For other persons, the period follows the earlier of the date the person last supplied services or materials, the date the contract is completed, abandoned or terminated, and the date a subcontract is certified complete. (Construction Act, s. 31 (2) (b), (3) (b))

Separate rules apply to the lien of the trustee of a workers' trust fund. A person who supplied services or materials both before and after substantial performance has separate liens, and the earlier one can expire without affecting the later one. (Construction Act, s. 31 (2.1), (4))

“No later than seven days after a contract is terminated, either the owner or the contractor or other person whose lien is subject to expiry shall publish a notice of the termination in the prescribed form and manner.” If a notice is published, the termination date for these expiry rules is the date it (or the first such notice) was published. This “does not prevent a person from contesting the validity of a termination.” (Construction Act, s. 31 (6)-(8))

“A lien may be preserved during the supplying of services or materials or at any time before it expires”. Where the lien attaches to the premises, this is done “by the registration in the proper land registry office of a claim for lien on the title of the premises”. Where it does not attach, it is done “by giving to the owner a copy of the claim for lien.” (Construction Act, s. 34 (1))

Where the owner is the Crown, the copy goes “to the prescribed office”, or if none is prescribed, to the ministry or Crown agency for whom the improvement is made. Where the owner is a municipality, it goes “to the clerk of the municipality.” For a railway right-of-way, it goes to “the manager or any person apparently in charge of any office of the railway in Ontario.” (Construction Act, s. 34 (3), (3.1), (4))

sections.heading: Perfecting a lien
paragraphs: “A lien may not be perfected unless it is preserved.” “A lien that has been preserved expires unless it is perfected prior to the end of the 90-day period next following the last day, under section 31, on which the lien could have been preserved.” (Construction Act, s. 36 (1), (2))

Where the lien attaches to the premises, it is perfected “when the lien claimant commences an action to enforce the lien” and, unless an order vacating the registration is made, “registers a certificate of action in the prescribed form on the title of the premises”. Where it does not attach, it is perfected when the claimant “commences an action to enforce the lien.” A preserved lien can also be perfected by “sheltering” under another claimant's perfected lien, under the rules in the Act. (Construction Act, s. 36 (3), (4))

“A perfected lien expires immediately after the second anniversary of the commencement of the action that perfected the lien”, unless, on or before that anniversary, an order is made for the trial of an action in which the lien may be enforced, or such an action “is set down for trial.” (Construction Act, s. 37 (1))
“The expiration of a lien under this Act shall not affect any other legal or equitable right or remedy otherwise available to the person whose lien has expired.” (Construction Act, s. 38)

sections.heading: Where lien actions are heard
paragraphs: “A lien claim is enforceable in an action in the Superior Court of Justice.” Except where inconsistent with the Act and its prescribed procedures, “the Courts of Justice Act and the rules of court apply to actions under this Part.” (Construction Act, s. 50)

After all statements of defence are delivered, or the time for delivering them has expired, a judge may, on motion, refer all or part of the action for trial to an associate judge, to a person agreed on by the parties, or, “if the action is for an amount that is within the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court”, to a deputy judge of that Court or to the Small Claims Court Administrative Judge. (Construction Act, s. 58 (1))
A reference to a person agreed on by the parties “shall not be made unless the persons entitled to notice under subsection (1.1) consent to the reference.” (Construction Act, s. 58 (1.1), (1.2))

sections.heading: Prompt payment
paragraphs: A “proper invoice” is “a written bill or other request for payment for services or materials in respect of an improvement under a contract” that contains information the Act lists, such as the contractor's name and address, the invoice date and a description of what was supplied, and meets any other requirements the contract specifies. “Proper invoices shall be given to an owner on a monthly basis, unless the contract provides otherwise.” (Construction Act, ss. 6.1 (1), 6.3 (1))

An invoice missing required information is treated as a proper invoice unless, “no later than seven days after receiving the invoice, the owner notifies the contractor in writing of the deficiency and of what is required to address it.” (Construction Act, s. 6.1 (2))

Subject to a notice of non-payment, an owner “shall pay the amount payable under a proper invoice no later than 28 days after receiving the proper invoice from the contractor.” An owner who disputes an invoice may refuse to pay if, “no later than 14 days after receiving the proper invoice”, it gives a notice of non-payment, in the prescribed form and manner, “specifying the amount of the proper invoice that is not being paid and detailing all of the reasons for non-payment.” (Construction Act, s. 6.4 (1), (2))
Any amount under the proper invoice that is not the subject of the owner's notice of non-payment is still to be paid within the 28 days. (Construction Act, s. 6.4 (3))

A contractor who receives full payment of a proper invoice within those 28 days pays each subcontractor whose services or materials were in the invoice “no later than seven days after receiving payment”. If the owner pays only part, the contractor pays those subcontractors from the amount paid, within the same seven days. Both are subject to a notice of non-payment and, like every payment under this Part, “subject to any requirement to retain a holdback”. (Construction Act, ss. 6.2, 6.5 (1), (2))

If the owner does not pay some or all of a proper invoice on time, the contractor pays those subcontractors “no later than 35 days after giving the proper invoice to the owner”, unless it gives a notice of non-payment. A notice given because the owner has not paid must include “an undertaking to refer the matter to adjudication under Part II.1 no later than 21 days after giving the notice to the subcontractor”. (Construction Act, s. 6.5 (4), (5))

A contractor who disputes a subcontractor's entitlement may instead give a notice “specifying the amount that is not being paid and detailing all of the reasons for non-payment.” The contractor's notice is due no later than seven days after receiving the owner's notice of non-payment or, if the owner gave none, before the 35-day period expires. Similar rules apply between subcontractors. (Construction Act, ss. 6.5 (6), (7), 6.6)

sections.heading: Adjudication
paragraphs: “Adjudication” means “construction dispute interim adjudication under this Part”. A party to a contract “may refer a dispute with the other party to the contract respecting any prescribed matter or any matter agreed to by the parties to adjudication.” The same applies to a subcontract. (Construction Act, ss. 13.1, 13.5 (1), (2))

For a contract, adjudication “may not be commenced if the notice of adjudication is given more than 90 days after the date on which the contract is completed, abandoned or terminated, unless the parties to the adjudication agree otherwise.” For a subcontract, the 90 days run from the earliest of that date, “the date on which the subcontract is certified to be completed under section 33”, and “the date on which the subcontractor last supplies services or materials to the improvement.” (Construction Act, s. 13.5 (3), (3.1))

A dispute may be referred to adjudication “even if the dispute is the subject of a court action or of an arbitration under the Arbitration Act, 1991, unless the action or arbitration has been finally determined.” An adjudication may only address a single dispute, unless the parties and the adjudicator agree otherwise. (Construction Act, s. 13.5 (4), (5))

Except as provided by the regulations, a written notice of adjudication includes the parties' names and addresses, “the nature and a brief description of the dispute, including details respecting how and when it arose”, “the nature of the redress sought”, “the name of a proposed adjudicator to conduct the adjudication”, and “the date, nature and substance of any previous adjudication in which the party was involved in respect of the contract or subcontract, including a copy of any determination made by the adjudicator.” (Construction Act, s. 13.7 (1))

The adjudicator decides “no later than 30 days after receiving the documents required by section 13.11”. Before it expires, that deadline may be extended by no more than 14 days on the adjudicator's request with the parties' written consent, or by the parties' written agreement with the adjudicator's consent. A determination made after the deadline “is of no force or effect.” (Construction Act, s. 13.13 (1), (2), (5))

The determination “is binding on the parties to the adjudication until a determination of the matter by a court”, an arbitration under the Arbitration Act, 1991, or a written agreement between the parties. A party required to pay “shall pay the amount no later than 15 days after the determination has been communicated to the parties to the adjudication”, subject to any requirement to retain a holdback. (Construction Act, ss. 13.15 (1), 13.19 (1), (2))

Judicial review of a determination “may only be made with leave of the Divisional Court”, and the motion for leave is filed, with proof of service, “no later than 35 days after the determination is communicated to the parties.” The determination may only be set aside on the grounds the Act lists. An application for judicial review “does not operate as a stay of the operation of the determination unless the Divisional Court orders otherwise.” (Construction Act, s. 13.18 (1), (2), (5), (7))

Subject to section 13.17, the parties “shall bear their own costs of the adjudication.” Under section 13.17, if the adjudicator determines a party acted in a manner that is “frivolous, vexatious, an abuse of process or other than in good faith”, the adjudicator may require that party to pay some or all of the other party's costs, part of the adjudicator's fee the other party would otherwise pay, or both. (Construction Act, ss. 13.16, 13.17)
